passages.happening:
Jesus says to his disciples, “It is inevitable that stumbling blocks will come, but woe to the one through whom they come!” (verse 1). “It would be better for him to have a millstone hung around his neck and to be thrown into the sea than to cause one of these little ones to stumble” (verse 2).

“Watch yourselves. If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him” (verse 3). Even if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times comes back and says, ‘I repent’, you must forgive him.
passages.hearers:
A ‘stumbling block’ is anything that trips a person up and makes them fall, here, fall away from God. Jesus says such things will come in a broken world. But that is no excuse for the one who causes them.

A millstone was the heavy round stone used to grind grain. Mark and Matthew speak of the great millstone turned by a donkey (Mark 9:42; Matthew 18:6); Luke says simply a stone of a mill. Either way, a man with one hung round his neck would never come up again.

‘These little ones’ are the weak and the vulnerable among Jesus' followers: children, and also new believers and anyone easily hurt or misled. Jesus' fiercest warning is for those who harm them.

Then he turns to life among his followers. ‘Watch yourselves’ can go with the warning before it or with the teaching after it; either way it calls for care. If a brother or sister sins against you, do not pretend nothing happened. Tell them. If they turn back, forgive them. And keep forgiving. ‘Seven times in a day’ is not a number to count up to. In the Bible seven is the number of fullness. Later Jewish teaching, written down centuries afterwards, records a rabbi's view that a person is forgiven three times for the same sin, but not a fourth. Jesus will not set any such limit. Matthew gives the same teaching in a longer form, with Peter's question and the parable of the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:21-35).
passages.ot: The Law already joined honesty and love: “You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart. Directly rebuke your neighbor, so that you will not incur guilt on account of him” (Leviticus 19:17). The next verse is the command, “Love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). To say what is wrong, and to forgive when the other turns, are both part of love.
passages.hard:
These words have been rightly applied to the abuse of children. It must be said plainly. This passage stands with the child. Jesus' fiercest warning in the Gospels is for anyone who harms a little one. The church has sometimes protected abusers and silenced children, and that is a betrayal of this very passage. Abuse of a child is a crime. It is to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, not handled quietly inside a church. If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now. If you were harmed as a child, what was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault.

Does ‘forgive him’ mean going back to someone who keeps hurting you? No. Forgiveness has also been misused. Some have told people who were abused to forgive quickly, keep quiet, or go back to the person who hurt them. That is not what this passage asks. Forgiveness lets go of revenge. It is not the same as trusting someone again, and it does not mean a crime should go unreported. A person can forgive and still stay safe, still tell the truth, and still ask for justice. It can also take a long time, and that is not failure.

Notice too that Jesus first says ‘rebuke him’. Forgiveness does not mean calling a wrong right. It names the wrong and then refuses to hold it over the other person. And the person who says ‘I repent’ seven times a day for the same harm, and keeps doing it, has not turned at all. Words alone do not make it safe to stay.
passages.asks: Ask whether anything in your life, your words, your example, your silence, has made it harder for someone weaker to trust God. Then ask whether there is someone you have been keeping a count against. Jesus asks you to let go of revenge. He does not ask you to stop being wise or safe.

passages.happening:
The apostles say to the Lord, “Increase our faith!” (verse 5).

He answers, “If you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it will obey you” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The apostles ask for more faith right after hearing that they must forgive seven times a day. That makes sense. Forgiving like that seems to need a giant faith.

Jesus' answer turns their request around. They do not need a bigger faith. A mustard seed was proverbially tiny (13:19). Even faith that small, if it is real faith in God, can do what seems impossible.

The tree is the mulberry. Most scholars think Luke means the black mulberry, a tree known for its deep, strong roots. To pull one up by a word, and then plant it in the sea, where no tree can grow, is a picture of the impossible. Matthew and Mark use a mountain thrown into the sea instead (Matthew 17:20; Mark 11:23). Both are pictures, not plans for moving trees.
passages.ot: God's people learned long ago that what matters is not the size of their strength but the strength of their God: “‘Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit,’ says the LORD of Hosts” (Zechariah 4:6).
passages.hard: Does this mean that enough faith will get you whatever you ask, and that if a prayer goes unanswered your faith was too small? No. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. The point of the mustard seed is that it is tiny. Jesus is not setting a level of faith that a person must reach to get results. Faith is trust in a person, not a payment that buys a cure. Its power is in the God it trusts, not in how strongly it is felt. This verse is not a formula, and it should never be used to blame anyone for a prayer that seems unanswered.
passages.asks: The apostles thought they needed more faith. Jesus told them to use the little they had. Ask what seems impossible to you right now, forgiving someone, perhaps, or letting go of something with deep roots. Bring your small faith to the God who is not small.

passages.happening:
Jesus asks, which of you, if your servant came in from ploughing or looking after the sheep, would say, ‘Come at once and sit down to eat’? Would you not rather say, ‘Prepare my meal and dress yourself to serve me while I eat and drink; and afterward you may eat and drink’ (verse 8)? Do you thank the servant for doing what he was told?

“So you also, when you have done everything commanded of you, should say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty’” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke gives this picture.

The word for ‘servant’ means a slave. In the Roman world slaves were part of ordinary households, and even a small farmer might own one who ploughed, kept the sheep and cooked. Everyone listening knew how such a household worked: when the slave came in from the field, he served the meal before he ate. Jesus uses a picture his hearers knew. He is not approving slavery, and he is not describing how God treats people. He is making one point. Obeying God does not put God in our debt.

The word translated ‘unworthy’ means ‘without claim’ or ‘owed nothing’. Older Bibles have ‘unprofitable’. The servants are not saying they are worthless. They are saying they have done what they were asked, and that their obedience is not a bill to send to God.

This is the opposite of a religion that keeps score: I prayed, I gave, I served, so God owes me. Jesus has just warned about people who think that way, and he will tell a story about one in the next chapter (18:9-14).
passages.ot: The psalmist asks, “How can I repay the LORD for all His goodness to me?” (Psalm 116:12). His answer is not a payment but thanks: “I will lift the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD” (Psalm 116:13). God's people serve him because he first saved them, not so that he will owe them.
passages.hard:
Does Jesus want his followers to think they are worthless? No. This saying is not a call to self-contempt. Notice what else Jesus says about masters and servants in Luke. In an earlier story the master comes home, “he will dress himself to serve and will have them recline at the table, and he himself will come and wait on them” (12:37). And at the Last Supper Jesus says, “But I am among you as one who serves” (22:27). The God who could ask for everything chooses to serve us. That is grace.

So the servants in verse 10 are not ashamed. They are free. They do not need to earn their place, because they cannot. They do their work and leave the reward to God. If you have been taught to see yourself as worthless, hear this: in the Bible you are made in God's image and loved enough that his Son came to serve you. ‘Unworthy’ here means only that you cannot put God in your debt. It does not mean you are of no worth to him.
passages.asks: Ask whether you have ever kept a quiet list of what God owes you for your service. Then set it down. You can serve without counting, because your place at his table does not depend on it.

passages.t: Ten lepers, and the one who came back
passages.happening:
On his way to Jerusalem, Jesus is passing between Samaria and Galilee. As he enters a village, ten men with leprosy meet him. They stand at a distance and shout, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!” (verse 13).

He sees them and says, “Go, show yourselves to the priests” (verse 14). On the way, they are cleansed.

One of them, seeing he is healed, comes back, praising God in a loud voice. He throws himself face down at Jesus' feet and thanks him. And he was a Samaritan.

“Were not all ten cleansed?” Jesus asks. “Where then are the other nine? Was no one found except this foreigner to return and give glory to God?” (verses 17-18). And he says to the man, “Rise and go; your faith has made you well!” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this story.

Biblical ‘leprosy’ was not the disease we now call leprosy (Hansen's disease). The Hebrew word covered a range of skin conditions, and even mould on cloth or walls. What made it terrible was not mainly pain. It was exclusion. The Law said, “He must live alone in a place outside the camp” (Leviticus 13:46). So the ten stand at a distance and shout.

Ten men shut out together. One of them was a Samaritan. The Samaritans worshipped the God of Israel and kept the five books of Moses, but at their own mountain, Gerizim, and Jews and Samaritans had a long history of bad feeling and violence on both sides (see the note on 9:51-56). Sickness and shame had thrown these men together across that old line. Jesus heals them all.

He sends them to the priests before anything has happened. Under the Law, a priest examined a person whose skin disease had healed and declared them clean, so that they could go home and worship again (Leviticus 14). The ten have to walk away still sick, trusting his word. And on the way they are cleansed.

Nine go on, perhaps to the priest, as they were told. They are not wicked; they are doing what Jesus said. But one turns back. He has seen something the others did not stop to see: the healing came from Jesus, and God should be thanked for it, loudly, face down in the dust.

The word Jesus uses for ‘foreigner’ is rare. It appears only here in the New Testament. It is the same Greek word carved on the stone warnings that stood around the inner courts of the temple in Jerusalem, forbidding any foreigner to go further on pain of death; one of them, found in 1871, still survives. The man that word kept out of the temple is the one who comes back to give glory to God.

‘Your faith has made you well’ can also be translated ‘your faith has saved you’. All ten were cleansed. One heard that he was saved.
passages.ot:
This story has an echo in the prophets. Naaman, a foreign army commander with a skin disease, was told by Elisha to wash in the Jordan. He obeyed, “and his flesh was restored and became like that of a little child, and he was clean” (2 Kings 5:14). Then he “went back to the man of God” and said, “Now I know for sure that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel” (2 Kings 5:15). Jesus had already pointed to Naaman in his first sermon (4:27). Once again the outsider is the one who comes back.

And the psalms call for thanks: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds” (Psalm 103:2).
passages.hard:
Were the nine punished for not coming back? The story does not say so. They were healed, and their healing was not taken away. Jesus' question is not a threat; it is a sorrowful wonder. Nine were cleansed and went on with their lives. One was cleansed and also came to know who had cleansed him.

This passage is also not a lesson against Jews, as if the nine stood for one people and the Samaritan for another. Jesus himself was a Jew, and he healed all ten. The story praises an outsider's gratitude, as the Good Samaritan praised an outsider's mercy (10:30-37). Samaritans are not only people in an old story. A small Samaritan community, about nine hundred people, still lives today.
passages.asks: It is easy to be one of the nine: to receive help, get better, and move on without a word. Ask what good things in your life you have never thanked God for. Then go back, as the Samaritan did, and say it aloud.

passages.t: ‘The kingdom of God is in your midst’
passages.happening:
Some Pharisees ask Jesus when the kingdom of God will come.

He replies, “The kingdom of God will not come with observable signs. Nor will people say, ‘Look, here it is,’ or ‘There it is.’ For you see, the kingdom of God is in your midst” (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
Many in Jesus' day longed for the kingdom of God, the time when God would set the world right and rule as king. Some looked for signs in the sky or in world events that would show it was near. The Pharisees ask when.

Jesus says it will not come in a way you can track on a chart or point to on a map. And then he says something startling: it is already here.

The Greek words behind ‘in your midst’ are hard to translate. The word entos most often means ‘inside’, and it means that in its only other use in the New Testament (Matthew 23:26). So older English Bibles such as the King James Version have ‘the kingdom of God is within you’. But the word can also mean ‘among’ or ‘within your reach’, and most modern translations, the BSB among them, choose ‘in your midst’ or ‘among you’. Many read it this way because Jesus is speaking to Pharisees who were opposing him, and because in Luke the kingdom is present in Jesus himself: “if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (11:20).
passages.ot: The prophets promised a day when God would reign: Daniel saw “One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven” (Daniel 7:13), given a kingdom that would never end. Many expected that day to come with plain signs. Jesus says the kingdom has come in a way they did not expect: in him, standing among them.
passages.hard:
So is the kingdom ‘within you’ or ‘in your midst’? Christians have read it in more than one way. Some, with the King James Version and much of the church's tradition of prayer, read it as God's reign in the heart, received inwardly. They point out that ‘inside’ is the word's usual meaning. Others read it as ‘among you’: the kingdom is present because the King is present, standing before them. They point to the context, a reply to opponents and a contrast with ‘Here it is’ and ‘There it is’. Some hold both: the kingdom is present in Jesus, and it is received by faith in the heart. Careful scholars hold each view, and these notes do not choose.

What neither reading allows matters too. The verse does not teach that the kingdom of God is simply a spark of the divine in every person, or our own human potential, with no need of the King who brings it. In Luke the kingdom is always tied to Jesus. And it does not allow anyone to set dates or read the news as a timetable for the end.
passages.asks: The Pharisees were looking for signs and missed the one standing in front of them. Ask where you have been looking for God in the spectacular and missing him in the ordinary: in Scripture, at the table, in the poor, in prayer. And ask whether you have let the King rule in you, not only around you.

passages.t: The days of the Son of Man: like Noah and Lot
passages.happening:
Then Jesus says to his disciples, “The time is coming when you will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man, but you will not see it” (verse 22). People will say, “Look, there He is!” or “Look, here He is!” Do not go out after them. As the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one end to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day. “But first He must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation” (verse 25).

It will be as in the days of Noah. People were eating and drinking, marrying and being given in marriage, up to the day Noah went into the ark. Then the flood came and destroyed them all. It was the same in the days of Lot. People were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building. But on the day Lot left Sodom, fire and sulphur rained down from heaven and destroyed them all. “It will be just like that on the day the Son of Man is revealed” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
Jesus has just told the Pharisees that the kingdom is already here. Now he tells his disciples that there is more to come: a day when he, ‘the Son of Man’, will be revealed openly. Jesus often used that title for himself. It comes from Daniel's vision of one ‘like the Son of Man’ who receives everlasting rule from God.

Matthew gives much of this teaching in Jesus' long talk on the Mount of Olives (Matthew 24:23-41). Luke places it here, on the road to Jerusalem, and adds things Matthew does not have: Lot and Sodom, the warning ‘Remember Lot's wife’, and the disciples' question at the end.

Two things are said together. First, no one will need to be told where he is. His coming will be as plain as lightning across the whole sky. So whoever says ‘He is here’ or ‘He is there’ is not to be followed. Second, before that day, ‘He must suffer many things’. The road to glory runs through the cross.

Noah's neighbours and the people of Sodom were not doing anything strange. They ate, married, traded, farmed and built. Their sin, in this saying, is that they lived as if nothing would ever change and God would never act. The day came suddenly, in the middle of ordinary life.
passages.ot: The story of the flood ends: “they were blotted out from the earth, and only Noah and those with him in the ark remained” (Genesis 7:23). And when Lot's family was led out of Sodom, the angels said, “Run for your lives! Do not look back, and do not stop anywhere on the plain!” (Genesis 19:17).
passages.hard:
Is Jesus giving a timetable for the end? No. He says the opposite: the day will come like lightning and like the flood, without warning. This stands against every attempt to set a date for the end. Many have tried, and every one has been wrong. Jesus told his disciples again after his resurrection, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by His own authority” (Acts 1:7). When Jesus will return is a question on which faithful Christians differ. That he will return is confessed by all.

Is it wrong to eat, marry, buy and build? No. These are good gifts, and Jesus did most of them himself. The danger is living as if they were all there is.
passages.asks: Noah's neighbours were busy with ordinary life, and ordinary life became their whole world. Ask what fills your days so completely that you rarely think of God at all. You do not need to stop living. You need to live as someone who expects the Lord.

passages.t: ‘Remember Lot's wife!’ One taken, one left
passages.happening:
“On that day, let no one on the housetop come down to retrieve his possessions. Likewise, let no one in the field return for anything he has left behind” (verse 31). “Remember Lot’s wife!” (verse 32). “Whoever tries to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will preserve it” (verse 33).

“I tell you, on that night two people will be in one bed: one will be taken and the other left. Two women will be grinding grain together: one will be taken and the other left” (verses 34-35).

“Where, Lord?” they ask. Jesus answers, “Wherever there is a carcass, there the vultures will gather” (verse 37).
passages.hearers:
Houses had flat roofs, used for work and rest. On that day, Jesus says, do not go back in for your things. Do not run back from the field for your coat. Nothing you own will matter.

Lot's wife is the warning. She was led out of Sodom, but she looked back, “and she became a pillar of salt” (Genesis 19:26). Her heart was still in the city she was leaving. Jesus' saying about losing and saving your life (compare 9:24) explains her: she tried to hold on, and lost everything.

Grinding grain on a hand mill was daily work in every home, and here two women do it together. ‘Two people in one bed’ and ‘two women grinding’ are pictures of people who share the closest life, at night and by day. Yet on that day they will be divided.

Verse 36. Older Bibles, such as the King James Version, have a verse here about two men in the field, one taken and the other left. The oldest copies of Luke, among them a papyrus called P75 and Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, do not have it. Many scholars think a copyist brought it in from Matthew, where the words appear: “Two men will be in the field: one will be taken and the other left” (Matthew 24:40). Others think a copyist's eye may have skipped it by accident, since verses 35 and 36 end with the same words. So the BSB, like most modern Bibles, leaves the number 36 empty and gives the words in a footnote. Nothing in Christian teaching turns on it.

The answer to ‘Where?’ sounds like a common saying: where there is a dead body, the birds gather. The Greek word can mean ‘eagles’ or ‘vultures’. Matthew uses the same saying (Matthew 24:28).
passages.ot: The book of Job says of the bird of prey, “where the slain are, there he is” (Job 39:30). Jesus uses a picture of the same kind: you will not need to ask where; it will be as plain as birds circling over a carcass.
passages.hard:
What does ‘one will be taken and the other left’ mean? Christians read it in two main ways. Many read it as the rapture: believers are suddenly taken to be with Christ, and others are left behind. The word rapture comes from the Latin for ‘caught up’ in 1 Thessalonians 4:17, “we who are alive and remain will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air.” Others read it the opposite way. In Noah's day and Lot's, it was the people destroyed who were taken, in judgment, and Noah and Lot who were left, safe. Luke's version adds the disciples' question, ‘Where, Lord?’, and Jesus' answer about vultures gathering at a body, which points to judgment. Christians also differ on when such a taking happens and how it fits with other passages. These notes do not choose, and they set out no end-times scheme. Both readings agree on Jesus' own point: the coming will be sudden, it will divide people who stood side by side, and the only wise thing is to be ready now.

No one can be ready for someone else. Two people in one bed share almost everything, but not this. Faith is not borrowed from a husband, a wife, a parent or a church.

These words are not given to make anyone afraid, least of all a child lying awake at night. They were spoken by the Lord who “must suffer many things” (verse 25) for the people he warns. His warning is a kindness: it comes while there is still time.
passages.asks: Lot's wife was leaving, but her heart stayed behind. Ask what you would look back for if God called you to leave it. And ask whether you are ready for the Lord today, not by fear, but by belonging to him now.
